content: 1. A study published in the Irish Medical Journal in 2004 (Volume 97, Pages 268–270) explored healthcare providers' perspectives on breastfeeding patterns among Pacific Islander mothers. Another study in the Journal of Midwifery & Women’s Health (2010; 55(2):162–170) by Flood JL and Dodgson JE examined the descriptions of breastfeeding practices among this population. 2. Bergh AM (1993) identified barriers and motivations for successful breastfeeding in a study published in Curationis (Volume 16, Issue 2, Pages 24–29). Similarly, Fuber CM and Thomson AM (2008) conducted a qualitative study on the emotional challenges faced by English midwives when integrating breastfeeding knowledge into practice, published in the International Journal of Nursing Studies (Volume 45, Pages 286–297). 3. Nelson AM (2007) investigated maternal-newborn nurses' experiences with inconsistent professional breastfeeding support in the Journal of Advanced Nursing (Volume 60, Issue 1, Pages 29–38). Becker GE (1992) assessed the breastfeeding knowledge of hospital staff in rural maternity units in Ireland, as reported in the Journal of Human Lactation (Volume 8, Pages 137–142). 4. Karnawat BS et al. (1987) studied hospital employees' knowledge and attitudes regarding infant feeding practices in Indian Pediatrics (Volume 24, Pages 939–948). Ouyang YQ et al. (2012) conducted a survey on breastfeeding practices among Chinese female physicians and nurses, published in Nursing & Health Sciences (Volume 14, Pages 298–303). 5. Lazzaro E et al. (1995) explored medical professionals' attitudes toward breastfeeding in the Journal of Human Lactation (Volume 11, Issue 2, Pages 97–101). Freed GL et al. (1995) conducted a national study on pediatricians' involvement in breastfeeding promotion, published in Pediatrics (Volume 96, Issue 3, Pages 490–494). 6. Freed GL et al. (1992) also examined pediatric house staff's attitudes and education concerning breastfeeding in the Southern Medical Journal (Volume 85, Pages 483–485). Lawrence RA (1982) reviewed medical professionals' practices and attitudes toward breastfeeding in Pediatrics (Volume 70, Issue 6, Pages 912–920). 7. Haager-Bürkert H et al. (2010) analyzed perceived challenges faced by German maternity clinics in obtaining Baby-Friendly Hospital certification, as reported in Geburtshilfe Frauenheilkunde (Volume 70, Issue 9, Pages 726–731). Szucs KA et al. (2009) studied breastfeeding knowledge, attitudes, and practices among providers in a medical home, published in Breastfeeding Medicine (Volume 4, Pages 31–42). 8. Ward KN and Byrne JP (2011) critically reviewed the impact of continuing breastfeeding education for nurses and midwives in the Journal of Human Lactation (Volume 27, Issue 4, Pages 381–393). Fuber CM and Thomson AM (2006) examined deviations and good practices in baby-feeding practices in the UK, published in Midwifery (Volume 22, Pages 365–376). 9. Moore T et al. (2007) discussed the implementation of the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative in New Zealand public hospitals in the International Breastfeeding Journal (Volume 2, Article 8). Cantrill RM et al. (2003) conducted an Australian study on midwives' breastfeeding knowledge, published in Midwifery (Volume 19, Pages 310–317). 10. Ekström A et al. (2005) investigated breastfeeding attitudes among counseling health professionals in the Scandinavian Journal of Public Health (Volume 33, Pages 353–359). Ellis DJ and Hewat RJ (1983) explored whether nurses help or hinder breastfeeding mothers in the Journal of Advanced Nursing (Volume 8, Pages 281–288). 11. Hellings P and Howe C (2000) assessed the breastfeeding knowledge of nurse practitioners and nurse-midwives in the Journal of Midwifery & Women’s Health (Volume 45, Pages 264–270). Krogstrand KS and Parr K (2005) highlighted physicians' need for problem-solving information to promote breastfeeding in the Journal of the American Dietetic Association (Volume 105, Pages 1943–1947). 12. Goldstein AO and Freed GL (1992) examined breastfeeding counseling practices among family practice residents in Family Medicine (Volume 25, Pages 524–529). Minnie CS and Greeff M (2006) studied baby-feeding choices in the context of the HIV/AIDS epidemic, published in Curationis (Volume 29, Issue 4, Pages 19–27). 13. Taveras EM et al. (2004) explored clinicians' opinions and practices associated with exclusive breastfeeding continuation in Pediatrics (Volume 113, Pages e283–e290). Wallace LM and Kosmala-Anderson J (2006) conducted a training needs survey of doctors' breastfeeding support skills in England, published in Maternal & Child Nutrition (Volume 2, Pages 217–231). 14. The World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines emphasize the importance of protecting, promoting, and supporting breastfeeding in facilities providing maternity and newborn services. These guidelines include recommendations on early skin-to-skin contact, rooming-in, demand feeding, and avoiding pacifiers or artificial teats to improve exclusive breastfeeding rates. 15. Systematic reviews, such as those by Moore ER et al. (2016) and Conde-Agudelo A et al. (2016), have assessed the effects of early skin-to-skin contact and kangaroo mother care on breastfeeding outcomes and infant health. These reviews highlight the benefits of these practices in improving breastfeeding initiation and reducing neonatal morbidity and mortality. 16. Studies by Smith E et al. (2017) and McFadden A et al. (2017) have further explored the impact of delayed breastfeeding initiation and additional breastfeeding support on infant survival and maternal practices. These findings underscore the importance of timely and effective breastfeeding interventions. 17. Research on rooming-in practices, such as that by Jaafar SH et al. (2016), demonstrates the positive impact of keeping mothers and infants together on breastfeeding duration. Similarly, Becker GE et al. (2016) reviewed methods of milk expression, emphasizing their safety, effectiveness, and cost implications. 18. The WHO guidelines also stress the need for written breastfeeding policies, staff training, and antenatal breastfeeding education to create an enabling environment for breastfeeding.
